opus-5.5.text:
I think it's quite promising, though it's still early. The main appeal is that diffusion models generate in a fundamentally different way from autoregressive models. An autoregressive LLM produces one token at a time, left to right, and once a token is out, it's committed. Diffusion works more like iterative refinement: you start with something noisy or masked and gradually clean it up across the whole sequence at once. That gives you a few potential advantages.

The first is parallelism and speed. If you can denoise many tokens at once, you may get much faster inference, especially for long outputs. Some of the recent diffusion-based language models have shown quite impressive throughput, and for applications like code generation, where latency matters a lot, that's a real selling point.

The second, which I find more interesting from a research point of view, is that diffusion naturally allows global planning and revision. Humans don't write strictly left to right. We sketch an outline, go back, fix things, restructure. Autoregressive models can only imitate that through tricks like chain-of-thought or self-correction prompts. A diffusion model has the ability to revise built into the generation process, so in principle it could be better at tasks that need the whole structure to be consistent: reasoning, planning, constraint satisfaction, certain kinds of math.

That said, there are real challenges. Autoregressive models benefit from a very clean training objective, next-token prediction, which scales extremely well, and we've built a huge ecosystem around it: KV caching, speculative decoding, RL fine-tuning pipelines, and so on. Diffusion language models have to catch up on all of that. Discrete diffusion over tokens is also trickier than continuous diffusion over images, and so far it's not fully clear whether diffusion LMs match autoregressive models in quality at the same scale, especially on hard reasoning.

So my view is that it's a very worthwhile direction, but probably not as a wholesale replacement in the short term. More likely we'll see hybrids: autoregressive at a coarse level with diffusion-style refinement locally, or diffusion used for drafting and an autoregressive model for verification. There's also a deeper theoretical question I care about: what is the right inductive bias for reasoning? Is sequential token-by-token generation actually necessary, or is it an artifact of how we started? Diffusion gives us a way to probe that question, and even if it doesn't win outright, I think we'll learn a lot about how these models represent and build up solutions.

r001.rationale: The response says denoising many tokens at once may make inference much faster and cites impressive throughput as a benefit.

r002.rationale: The response says it is unclear whether diffusion LMs match autoregressive models in quality at the same scale, but does not clearly state that they still lag behind leading LLMs in capability.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think it's a genuinely promising direction, but I'd separate the hype from the actual technical case.

The core appeal of diffusion for language is that you break out of the strictly left-to-right, token-by-token constraint of autoregressive models. You generate the whole sequence in parallel and refine it iteratively. That buys you a few things. First, you can in principle get much higher throughput, because each denoising step produces many tokens at once instead of one. Second, you get a natural way to do things like infilling, editing, and planning, where you want to settle the global structure of an answer first and then fill in details. Autoregressive models do that implicitly and sometimes awkwardly. A diffusion model does it by construction. Third, there's a nice connection to reasoning. A lot of hard problems, things like puzzles, code with constraints, or planning tasks, are really about satisfying global constraints, and iterative refinement over the whole sequence feels like a more natural computational primitive for that than committing to tokens one by one.

That said, I'd be honest about the challenges. Text is discrete, and the diffusion machinery was built for continuous signals. The discrete and masked diffusion variants work, but the training objective is harder to make efficient, and historically these models have lagged autoregressive models in raw likelihood and quality at the same compute. The entire ecosystem, from KV caching to speculative decoding to RL post-training, is built around autoregressive generation, so the engineering gap is real. And some of the speed advantage shrinks when you realize you often need many refinement steps to match quality.

Where I think it gets interesting is the hybrid space. Autoregressive at the block or chunk level, diffusion within blocks. Or using diffusion as a planner or draft model and an autoregressive model as the verifier. Those combinations let you keep what works while gaining parallelism and global coherence. Recent results from several groups have shown that discrete diffusion language models can get surprisingly competitive, and once that happens, the speed and controllability advantages start to matter.

So my view is that it won't simply replace autoregressive models overnight, but it's one of the few directions that attacks the fundamental sequential bottleneck rather than just scaling around it. That's why I think it's worth serious investment.

r001.rationale: It identifies higher throughput as a potential benefit: each denoising step can produce many tokens at once, enabling faster generation.

r002.rationale: It says these models have historically lagged in likelihood and quality at the same compute, but does not clearly state that they still lag leading language models in capability.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a promising direction, especially because it gives us a different way to generate and refine an answer. Most language models generate text from left to right: once a token is produced, they keep going. A diffusion approach can potentially work on the whole sequence, gradually refining it. That opens up interesting possibilities for tasks where different parts of an answer need to be consistent with one another.

But there are some real challenges. Text is discrete, so the methods that work well for images don’t transfer directly. And parallel generation doesn’t automatically mean faster generation—if you need many rounds of refinement, that can still be expensive. You have to compare quality and computational cost together.

What interests me most is whether we can combine their strengths: use an autoregressive model to establish a structure, for example, and an iterative process to revise it. The key question is whether those revisions actually improve correctness and coherence, rather than just changing the wording. So I’m optimistic about exploring it, but I wouldn’t assume diffusion will simply replace the current approach.

r001.rationale: The response discusses whole-sequence refinement and cautions that parallel generation may still be expensive; it does not identify faster decoding as a promising benefit.

r002.rationale: The response mentions challenges with discrete text and computational cost, but does not say diffusion-based language models lag behind leading language models in capability.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s a promising direction, but we should distinguish between using diffusion to generate language and combining a language model with a diffusion model for images or video.

For language generation itself, the interesting question is whether we have to generate everything one token at a time. An autoregressive model commits to a sequence from left to right. A diffusion model can potentially start with a rough version and refine different parts together. That could be useful for tasks where you want to revise an entire answer or satisfy several constraints at once.

But there are challenges. Text is discrete, so the methods that work naturally for images don’t transfer directly. And parallel generation doesn’t automatically mean faster generation: if you need many rounds of refinement, you may lose that advantage. You also have to compare against very well-optimized autoregressive systems.

Combining the two approaches is interesting because they may have complementary strengths. A language model could help determine what to generate, while a diffusion process handles generation or refinement. My view is that it’s worth exploring, but the key is to find a task where that combination delivers a clear advantage in quality, efficiency, or control.

r001.rationale: The response describes parallel generation as a possibility but cautions that refinement rounds may erase any speed advantage. It does not clearly identify faster decoding as a promising benefit.

r002.rationale: The response says diffusion methods face challenges and should be compared with optimized autoregressive systems, but it does not state that diffusion-based language models lag behind leading models in capability.
